issue_context.title: [API Proposal]: Add formatting support to `System.Net.ServerSentEvents`
comments:
> +    public static SseFormatter Create<T>(IAsyncEnumerable<SseItem<T>> source, SseItemFormatter<T> itemFormatter);

Seems like this design forces a `byte[]` allocation for every item. What about writing it directly to the destination stream?

I noticed that our `SseItem` struct doesn't define a `retry` field. Should it since the underlying spec supports it as an optional property?

> This will introduce warnings into folks' code. Why is it necessary?

It seems like according to the spec, the event type is actually optional. We may introduce new warnings here but it strikes me as valid given the it's possible for the underlying value to be null. We're a lot more permissive about making non-nullable properties nullable in ASP.NET Core reviews so I tend to be more relax about introducing new warnings if they actually make sense. 😅

> Seems like this design forces a `byte[]` allocation for every item. 

I initially experimented with a signature matching that of [`IUtf8SpanFormattable`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.iutf8spanformattable.tryformat?view=net-8.0) but realized that it doesn't compose well with how most serializers work. A typical implementation would have to allocate its own `byte[]` which it then needs to compare against the destination buffer. If it doesn't fit, it would need to be rerun up until the point a matching destination has been provided.

> What about writing it directly to the destination stream?

We need a way to intercept line breaks. Maybe it's possible to do so by wrapping the underlying stream but I haven't tested this out. Worth a try you think?

```C#
public delegate ValueTask SseItemFormatter<T>(Stream stream, T value);
```

But not sure how well this would compose with a hypothetical future API that targets `PipeWriter`. Perhaps using `IBufferWriter<byte>` might be preferable here:

```C#
public delegate void SseItemFormatter<T>(IBufferWriter<byte> writer, T value);
```
cc: @dotnet/ncl since the bot was lazy

> It seems like according to the spec, the event type is actually optional

It is optional, and when it's not supplied, implementations are supposed to infer "message". So we exposed SseParser.EventTypeDefault, so that if it's not there in the wire data, the .NET representation of it can provide it explicitly.

If we want to make the ctor parameter optional and have the constructor supply "message" when the event type is null, I'm fine with that. But making the property be nullable doesn't seem warranted; it's just introducing friction. What's the case where someone is going to behave differently based on whether EventType returns null or returns "message"? Presumably we actually make it harder for consumers with this being nullable, as someone wanting to handle the default case needs to check for both null and "message".

> Presumably we actually make it harder for consumers with this being nullable, as someone wanting to handle the default case needs to check for both null and "message".

The downside of keeping it non-nullable is that we'd mandating event types to be written on the formatter side. Unless of course we use a separate type to model written events or decide that `"message"` is the magic string that results in event types being omitted.

> The downside of keeping it non-nullable is that we'd mandating event types to be written on the formatter side.

Why? If it returns "message", the formatter can choose to elide it. That's true whether or not the property can also return null.

> Why? If it returns "message", the formatter can choose to elide it. That's true whether or not the property can also return null.

So we make "message" a magic string?

> So we make "message" a magic string?

The spec makes it a magic string.

review_comments:
Is the `try-finally` here needed?
The array pool should handle dropped arrays in case of an exception.

> The array pool should handle dropped arrays in case of an exception.

How is that?

In case of an exception the array won't be returned to the pool, so ultimately it will be GCed.
That's no problem for the array pool, so the `try-finally` isn't needed.

In the previous comment the cited statement wasn't very clear -- sorry.

> In case of an exception the array won't be returned to the pool, so ultimately it will be GCed.

Why is that desirable? Why discard the buffer just because an exception was thrown?

The exception here isn't the common case, so one can avoid additional complexity brought by try-finally that is not needed.

The pattern with try-finally for the array pool was used at the beginning of AP, but recently renting / returning is just done w/o try-finally. See e.g. https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/71249#issuecomment-1165486832 and lots of other comments for this.
I don't think inserting a try/finally is so terrible from a code complexity standpoint. We use that pattern pervasively and I don't think we need to remove it here.

> We use that pattern pervasively

Really? Recently I see it the other way around.

But to shorten this discussion to whatever you think is right here.
I don't at all agree with that approach. Should we be starving the buffer pool just because of a transient network outage?

async operations aren't necessarily done referencing the buffer when they throw (it's possible the native half can write after the managed half throws a timeout exception, for example), so they're not supposed to return it except in successful flows.

> it's possible the native half can write after the managed half throws a timeout exception, for example

Can you give an example in the repo where that might happen?

In any case, we're using this pattern pervasively including in the SseParser class of this project:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/2c7c6bf5d18a7d42f4b9f48fe4bced22f1d292ae/src/libraries/System.Net.ServerSentEvents/src/System/Net/ServerSentEvents/SseParser_1.cs#L233-L240

If this turns out to be problematic, it would probably require a more systematic approach to fix it.

Could this use https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/src/libraries/Common/src/System/Net/ArrayBuffer.cs?
(looks like the same idea at a quick glance)
Looks similar, but AFAICT it doesn't implement IBufferWriter. FWIW this is duplicated from STJ so clearly we would benefit from a shared thing.

> FWIW this is duplicated from STJ so clearly we would benefit from a shared thing.

Duplicated, as in copy/paste? Can you move the code from STJ to a shared location and just include it in both then?
Yep. The STJ type implements `PipeWriter` instead of `IBufferWriter` so we can't just share the source without taking an extra dependency in pre 9.0 targets.

> Yep. The STJ type implements `PipeWriter` instead of `IBufferWriter` so we can't just share the source without taking an extra dependency in pre 9.0 targets.

And that's not a case of just having two partial files, one with this type implementing IBufferWriter and one with it also adding the PipeWriter derivation?

Or putting all of this logic into a shared type that's then just delegated to with one-liners from the two different wrappers?

There is a lot of non-trivial logic here. We should avoid copy/pasting it.
Thanks, this is a huge improvement.
